html:
The Kazakh famine of 1930 to 1933, called Asharshylyq in Kazakh, was a man-made famine in Soviet Kazakhstan. An estimated 1.3 to 2.3 million people died, most of them Kazakhs. Between 38 and 42 percent of all Kazakhs perished, the highest share of any people in the Soviet famines of those years.

It was a direct result of Soviet collectivisation. Kazakhs were mostly nomadic herders who lived by moving their flocks between seasonal pastures. Under the party chief Filipp Goloshchyokin, the state:

  • seized livestock and set impossible quotas for meat and grain
  • forced nomads to settle on collective farms that could not support them
  • blacklisted whole districts, cutting them off from trade

The herds collapsed; Kazakhstan lost most of its livestock. With no animals and no harvest, people starved. More than a million fled, to other Soviet regions, to China, Mongolia and Afghanistan. Border guards shot many who tried to cross into China.

The famine began in late 1930, a year before the worst of the Holodomor in Ukraine, and lasted into 1933. It came little more than a decade after the famine of 1919 to 1922.

It changed Kazakhstan for good. Kazakhs became a minority in their own republic until after independence, and the nomadic way of life was largely destroyed. Under Stalin the famine was hidden. Only in the late Soviet years could it be discussed openly; Kazakhstan now marks 31 May as a day of remembrance for the victims of political repression and famine.
